title: Removing a stone from the road
hookLine: taking harm out of a path is a branch of faith (Muslim)
tomorrow: Camp 3 close: a day with the practices

lines: A BROKEN BOTTLE ON THE SIDEWALK.
A WEEK OF CHARITY, SMALLER EACH DAY.
cards: There's a broken bottle in the middle of the sidewalk. Or a branch across the bike lane. Or a shopping cart abandoned in a parking space.
You could step around it. Everyone else has.

All week, charity has gotten a little smaller and a little closer: a smile, a secret gift, a welcome for someone new, eight addresses, a well that keeps flowing, the house next door. Today it gets as small as it goes.
Today: removing a stone from the road.

teach.b: Sahih Muslim reports the Prophet ﷺ saying: faith has seventy-some branches, or sixty-some; the narrator wasn't sure which.
The highest is saying la ilaha illallah, there is no god but Allah. The lowest is removing something harmful from the road. And modesty is a branch of faith.
Put those side by side: the testimony at the center of Islam, the words you met on day one hundred seventeen, and moving a stone out of the way. Same tree, different branches.
The smallest act is still faith, not a lesser thing to be embarrassed about. Bukhari and Muslim tell a story about it.
A man walking along a road found a thorny branch lying across it, and moved it aside. That's all. And the Prophet said Allah thanked him for it, and forgave him.
In another report in Muslim, the Prophet said he saw a man moving about freely in Paradise because of a tree he had cut away from the middle of a road, where it had been hurting people.
A companion named Abu Barzah once asked the Prophet: teach me something that will benefit me. The answer, in Sahih Muslim, wasn't a long devotion.
It was: remove what harms from the path of the Muslims. Notice who benefits: people you'll never meet. The cyclist who won't swerve.
The child who won't cut a foot. The old man who won't trip. They won't thank you, because they'll never know anything was there.
It's secret charity, done with your feet. Faith, at its smallest, is noticing the thing in the way, and moving it.

how: Muslims count removing anything harmful from a road or path, a stone, glass, a branch, as an act of faith and charity, following the hadith of the branches of faith.

o: a thorn bush planted to guard a garden's edge
the thorns Shaytan scatters to trip up the faithful
the obstacle a man moved off a road, and was forgiven

games.q: what's inside the stone on the road — tap the pairs.
p: asked to be taught something useful

s: the hadith puts removing harm from the road on the same tree as the testimony of faith
the highest branch is la ilaha illallah; the lowest, removing harm from the road (Muslim 35).
only big acts of charity count as faith
the lowest branch, moving harm out of the way, is still a branch of faith.
the man who moved the thorny branch was rewarded
Allah thanked him and forgave him (Bukhari, Muslim).

games.q: you're Abu Barzah. you ask the Prophet ﷺ to teach you something that will benefit you. what does he say?
o: pray a thousand units a night
remove harm from the path of the Muslims
games.why: remove harm from the path of the Muslims (Muslim 2618). the smallest act, for people you'll never meet.

practice: Picture the paths near you: your hallway, your front step, the sidewalk, a shared kitchen, the stairs at work.

Notice what's in the way, a box on the stairs, shoes in the doorway, a spill no one wiped, and how many small harms you usually step around without seeing. If you pray, you can intend moving one of them as a branch of faith.

wordCard.voice: Thorny branch. The hadith's man who moved one off the road, and was thanked and forgiven by Allah for it.

orig.note: Arabic: removing harm from the road, the lowest branch of faith.

carryVoice: Your line: clear the path. The lowest branch is still on the tree. Day one hundred fifty-five, done.
